Screen Macro · AI tab

Training a Detection Model

Five steps from an empty project to a trained model linked into your bot: capture example frames, label what's in them, hand off to free GPU training, and import the result.

Every step below is independently re-runnable. Capturing a few more frames later doesn't force you to relabel everything; re-labeling doesn't force a retrain. Come back to any project at any time and pick up wherever you left off.
1

Train New Model

Click Train New Model, bottom-left of the AI tab. Name it after what it should detect (e.g. coin, enemy_ship) — must be unique among your existing projects. This goes straight into Capture Frames once you click OK.

2

Capture Frames

Position the game (or emulator) to show the object, then press F9 — this works even while the game window itself is focused, not just Screen Macro — or click Capture Frame directly in the dialog. Repeat from different angles, zoom levels, and game states; more variety trains a more reliable model.

Close the dialog whenever you have enough (there's no fixed minimum — more frames, especially varied ones, generally means a more reliable model). You can always reopen Capture Frames later to add more.

Alternative: capture automatically while the bot runs. The Screen Editor tab has its own + Frame Capture AI action (next to + Detect Model, in a screen's AI actions row) — add it to any screen's flow and link it to one or more training projects, finished or still in progress:

Every time the running bot's scenario passes through that action, it captures the current frame straight into each linked project's dataset — no dedicated capture session needed, just growing the dataset passively while the bot runs through moments where the object is known to be visible.

3

Label Frames

Click Label Frames. The first time, you'll be asked whether to outline objects as a Bounding Box (drag a rectangle, faster) or a Polygon (trace the actual shape, tighter fit, slower) — this choice applies to the whole project going forward.

Drag a box around one instance of the object, then click the exact spot the bot should click on it. Repeat for every instance visible in that frame. If the object isn't visible at all, click Next Frame without drawing anything — that's recorded as a real negative example, which helps the model learn what isn't the object too, not just what is.

If you'd rather not draw every box by hand, the Settings tab's Labeling provider can be switched to Roboflow (SAM 3) — see the separate Roboflow tutorial. With that enabled, Auto-Label Settings… (a Roboflow-only row action) configures which class name(s) to search each frame for, each with its own confidence, plus the NMS IoU threshold:

With that configured, "Label Frames" instead fetches suggestions for the whole dataset in the background (a progress bar tracks it, bottom-right of the AI tab — the rest of the app stays usable while it runs) and saves them directly, unreviewed; use Review Labels (next step) to check them.

4

Review Labelsrecommended

Click Review Labels to step back through already-labeled frames and correct mistakes — opens straight on the first not-yet-reviewed frame, no prompt. Useful after Roboflow auto-labels a batch (nothing's been reviewed yet at that point), or just to double-check your own manual labeling before spending GPU time training on it.

The object list lets you select and remove one specific box or polygon, regardless of draw order — handy when only one of several objects in a frame is wrong. The frame-number box jumps straight to any frame; Previous/Next step one at a time. Leaving a frame any way (including closing the dialog) saves it and marks it reviewed.

5

Start Training

Click Start Training. First it asks which model architecture to train:

  • RF-DETR — also predicts the exact click point, not just a box; slower to train.
  • YOLO — box only (clicks the box center); faster to train and export.
  • The two (Segmentation) variants train on real mask supervision for potentially tighter box localization, but still export box-only — they're greyed out unless this project was labeled in Polygon mode, since a box-only dataset has nothing for the segmentation loss to train against.

Screen Macro then zips your captured/labeled frames and opens the matching training notebook in your browser (Colab by default — Kaggle is available too, opt-in via the Settings tab). This dialog tells you exactly what to do next and gives you a one-click Copy for the dataset zip's path:

In the notebook itself, the first cell explains exactly what this specific training run will do:

  1. Runtime → Change runtime type → pick a GPU (T4 is fine, free tier).
  1. Runtime → Run all.
  1. Colab will warn that the notebook "was not authored by Google" — expected for any notebook opened from a GitHub link rather than Google's own library. Click through it.
  2. Wait for a Choose files button to appear (installs dependencies first, can take a minute), click it, and select the dataset zip whose path you copied earlier.

Everything after that runs on its own — training, export, and an optional sanity check. The whole run can take anywhere from 30 minutes up to several hours; the actual training cell is by far the slowest part, a long wait there is expected, not a freeze. When it finishes, best.onnx downloads to your computer automatically.

6

Import Model

Back in Screen Macro's AI tab, select your project's row and click Import Model…. Browse to the best.onnx file Colab just downloaded (usually your Downloads folder) and select it — the Imported Model column fills in immediately.

That's it — the project now has a real trained model. Link it to a bot action from the Screen Editor's AI Actions section (+ Detect Model), picking this model by name from its dropdown (only finished, imported models show up there).

Iterating later

Model not reliable enough yet? Capture more frames (especially ones it seems to get wrong), label/review them, and Start Training again — each step picks up exactly where it left off, nothing needs to be redone from scratch.
